content.content:
The `check_same_thread` parameter is documented in the `sqlite3.connect()` parameter list:

> **check_same_thread** ([_bool_](../builtins/functions.html#bool "bool")) – If `True` (default), [`ProgrammingError`](#sqlite3.ProgrammingError "sqlite3.ProgrammingError") will be raised if the database connection is used by a thread other than the one that created it. If `False`, the connection may be accessed in multiple threads; write operations may need to be serialized by the user to avoid data corruption. See [`threadsafety`](#sqlite3.threadsafety "sqlite3.threadsafety") for more information.

So a connection is **not** shared across threads by default. Using it from another thread raises `ProgrammingError`. Setting `check_same_thread=False` allows multi-threaded access, but the documentation says write operations may need to be serialized by your code to avoid data corruption.

The `threadsafety` section explains what the underlying SQLite library supports. The page's mapping table gives these DB-API meanings:

- **multi-thread** (threadsafety 2): "Threads may share the module, but not connections"
- **serialized** (threadsafety 3): "Threads may share the module, connections and cursors"

The `threadsafety` value is set by the SQLite threading mode the library was compiled with, not by `check_same_thread`. The page also notes that since Python 3.11 it is set dynamically rather than hard-coded.

Example:

```python
import sqlite3
import threading

# Default: connection is bound to the creating thread
con = sqlite3.connect("tutorial.db")
# Using `con` from another thread raises ProgrammingError

# Opt in to cross-thread use; you must serialize writes yourself
lock = threading.Lock()
con = sqlite3.connect("tutorial.db", check_same_thread=False)

def write_row(title, year, score):
    with lock:
        con.execute("INSERT INTO movie VALUES(?, ?, ?)", (title, year, score))
        con.commit()
```

The short answer: `check_same_thread=False` lets one connection be used from several threads, but it doesn't make concurrent writes safe. You have to serialize them yourself.

**Default behavior:** By default the flag is True, and the connection can only be used by the thread that created it. Using it from another thread raises `ProgrammingError` ([GitHub issue 128697](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/128697)). A common case is IPython's history database, which hit this error when IPython ran in a thread. The fix there was to pass `check_same_thread=False` ([IPython changeset](https://code.rhodecode.com/upstream/ipython/changeset/2da6fb9870dffd838ba87b8e99ded17acd0d4edb)).

**What False gives you:** Setting it to False lets the connection be accessed from multiple threads. The docs still say that write operations may need to be serialized by your code to avoid data corruption ([GitHub issue 128697](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/128697)).

**Why serialization matters:** SQLite's serialized threading mode protects the library's internals, so threads won't damage the database file. But each connection has only one transaction in progress at a time. If two threads write through the same connection without a lock, their transactions can mix, and one thread's commit or rollback can affect the other's work ([Python docs tracker, issue 27113](https://www.python.org/pipermail/docs/2016-June/026751.html)).

**Safer patterns, from the same discussion:**
- Use a single dedicated writer thread, with other threads only reading.
- Wrap your transactions in a `threading.Lock`.
- Give each thread its own connection. In that case you don't need `check_same_thread=False` at all ([Python docs tracker, issue 27113](https://www.python.org/pipermail/docs/2016-June/026751.html)).

**Documentation history:** The sqlite3 docs were reworded in GH-101351 to describe the flag more precisely, including the note that `threadsafety` has more detail ([CPython commit](https://android.googlesource.com/platform/external/python/cpython3/+/f8abe755e8%5E%21)). A later issue asking whether the default should be changed was closed as not planned ([GitHub issue 128697](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/128697)).

A minimal pattern that works:

```python
import sqlite3, threading

conn = sqlite3.connect("app.db", check_same_thread=False)
lock = threading.Lock()

def save(row):
    with lock:          # one transaction at a time
        with conn:      # commits on success, rolls back on error
            conn.execute("INSERT INTO t (v) VALUES (?)", (row,))
```

content.text:
By default, a sqlite3 connection cannot be shared across threads: with `check_same_thread=True` (the default), using it from another thread raises `ProgrammingError`. Setting `check_same_thread=False` allows multi-thread access, and as the docs put it, "If `False`, the connection may be accessed in multiple threads; write operations may need to be serialized by the user to avoid data corruption."

Sources:
- [Python sqlite3 documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html)
- [GitHub issue 128697](https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/128697)
